title: Oleander
intro: Oleander keeps staging detachment before demonstrating how difficult it is. The speaker claims he can let go, promises to listen and asks the other person not to give up; only then do we learn that the feeling is one-sided and perhaps unknown to its recipient. Permission to leave offers a less possessive gesture in the middle, but it is not the ending. The song returns to the plea and finishes by naming the one-sided attachment again. Letting someone go has become imaginable without becoming emotionally complete.
reading: One-sided imagined conversation; permission to leave is a middle movement, not a resolved final outcome.

revisions.t44-n1: The proverb praises taking something on without becoming unable to put it down. The immediate plea not to give up shows that the second ability is still being rehearsed. Repetition does not make the self-description true; it makes the effort to inhabit it audible. Later permission to leave is a concrete gesture toward that ideal, but the returning attachment prevents it from becoming a clean story of mastery.
revisions.editorial-44-one-sided: This information changes the earlier address. A person can be asked not to give up inside the speaker's imagined conversation even when they do not know what they are being asked to preserve. The lyric gives us access to words that may never reach their apparent addressee. That is more specific than an ordinary breakup scene: the relationship sustaining the song may be much more developed on one side than the other.
revisions.editorial-44-unable-speak: The song can repeat a plea while describing someone unable to speak it. Singing is the form that makes the unsaid available to us, not proof that the other person has heard it. This distinction explains why the lyric contains both direct appeals and the admission that the feeling remains unknown. The empty head is a blockage at the moment of contact, not an absence of emotion.
revisions.editorial-44-leave-first: Permission to go removes blame from the other person, which is a meaningful change from asking them to stay. But it occurs midway through the song. The opening pleas return afterwards, and the final section again calls the feeling one-sided. The gesture is generous without being a completed release. Reading it as the closing resolution would mistake what the speaker can offer for what he has already managed to feel.
